weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best captures the principle of distributional semantics?

options.text: Words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings.
A word's meaning is fully fixed by its dictionary definition.
Meaning is determined solely by a word's spelling.
Distributional semantics has no connection to word embeddings.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings.

questions.prompt: Which of the following words is least likely to be polysemous?

options.text: Bank
Point
Oxygen
Head

questions.sourceAnswerText: Oxygen

questions.prompt:
Consider the following sentence pair:
Sentence 1: The cat chased the mouse.
Sentence 2: The mouse was caught.
Does Sentence 1 entail Sentence 2?

options.text: Yes
No

questions.sourceAnswerText: No

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains a homonym?

options.text: He filled the glass with water.
The bat flew out of the cave at dusk.
She painted the wooden fence white.
They walked slowly along the shore.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The bat flew out of the cave at dusk.

questions.prompt: Which of the following relationships is incorrectly labeled?

options.text: Petal is a holonym of flower.
Sparrow is a hyponym of bird.
Oak is a hyponym of tree.
Wheel is a meronym of car.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Petal is a holonym of flower.

questions.prompt: _________ studies how context influences the interpretation of meaning.

options.text: Syntax
Morphology
Pragmatics
Phonology

questions.sourceAnswerText: Pragmatics

questions.prompt: In the sentence, “After Meena scolded Priya, she walked away,” who does “she” most likely refer to?

options.text: Meena
Priya
Ambiguous
Neither

questions.sourceAnswerText: Ambiguous

questions.prompt:
Which of the following statements is true?
(i) Word embeddings capture semantic similarity through context.
(ii) A hyponym is more general than its hypernym.
(iii) Morphological analysis has no role in language modelling.

options.text: Only (i)
Only (i) and (ii)
Only (ii) and (iii)
All of the above

questions.sourceAnswerText: Only (i)

questions.prompt:
What issues can be observed in the following text?
“Loving this staycation vibe – feelin chill n totally zen, no worries!”

options.text: Idioms
Non-standard English
Tricky Entity Names
Neologisms

questions.sourceAnswerText: Non-standard English, Tricky Entity Names

questions.prompt: In semantic role labelling, we determine the semantic role of each argument with respect to the ___________ of the sentence.

options.text: noun phrase
subject
predicate
adjunct

questions.sourceAnswerText: predicate

questions.prompt: Which of the following has the least direct effect on a model's perplexity over a fixed test set?

options.text: Vocabulary size
Probability assigned to the test sentences
Number of tokens in the test set
Average sentence length

questions.prompt: What is the central task of a probabilistic language model?

options.text: Translating between languages
Assigning probabilities to word sequences (predicting the next word)
Clustering documents by topic
Extracting named entities

questions.sourceAnswerText: Assigning probabilities to word sequences (predicting the next word)

questions.prompt: Which equation correctly expresses the chain rule for a 3-word sentence?
Which assumption allows n-gram models to reduce computation?

options.text: Bayes Assumption
Chain Rule
Independence Assumption
Markov Assumption

questions.sourceAnswerText: Markov Assumption

questions.prompt: A model that conditions each word on the previous two words is equivalent to which Markov model?

options.text: First-order
Second-order
Third-order
Fourth-order

questions.sourceAnswerText: Second-order

questions.prompt: Which smoothing technique leverages the number of unique contexts a word appears in?

options.text: Good-Turing
Add-k
Kneser-Ney
Absolute Discounting

questions.sourceAnswerText: Kneser-Ney

questions.prompt:
For the question below, consider the following corpus:
<s> the river flows to sea </s>
<s> boats sail on the river </s>
<s> the sea is deep </s>

Assuming a bi-gram language model, calculate the probability of the sentence: the sea flows to river. (Ignore the unigram probability of P() in your calculation.)

For the question below, consider the following corpus:
<s> the river flows to sea </s>
<s> boats sail on the river </s>
<s> the sea is deep </s>

Assuming a bi-gram language model, calculate the perplexity of the sentence: the sea flows to river. (Do not consider <s> and </s> as words of the sentence.)

options.text: None of these

questions.prompt: Which component of a neural network introduces non-linearity into the model?

options.text: Weights
Bias
Activation function
Loss function

questions.sourceAnswerText: Activation function

questions.prompt: In backpropagation, which method is used to compute the gradients?

options.text: Gradient descent
Chain rule of derivatives
Matrix factorization
Linear regression

questions.prompt: Which of the following functions is not differentiable at zero?

options.text: Sigmoid
Tanh
ReLU
Linear

questions.prompt: Which activation function is least likely to suffer from vanishing gradients?

options.text: Tanh
Sigmoid
ReLU

questions.prompt: Which of the following equations correctly represents the derivative of the sigmoid function?

options.text: σ(x)²

questions.prompt: Why can a single-layer perceptron not solve the XOR problem?

options.text: XOR requires probabilistic outputs
XOR is non-linear and not linearly separable
XOR has more than two classes
XOR requires backpropagation

questions.prompt: Which type of regularization encourages sparsity in the weights?

options.text: L1 regularization
L2 regularization
Dropout
Early stopping

questions.sourceAnswerText: L1 regularization

options.text: It is applied with a higher probability
It is applied with a lower probability
It is disabled and all neurons are used
It is replaced by L2 regularization

options.text: Tanh
ReLU
Sigmoid
Softmax

options.text: Loss decreases smoothly
Loss oscillates or diverges
Loss always stays zero
None of these

weeks.title: Week 4
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: State True or False. In the Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) model, the surrounding context words are used to predict the centre target word.

options.text: True
False

questions.sourceAnswerText: True

questions.prompt: Two distinct words in a vocabulary are represented as one-hot vectors. What is the cosine similarity between them?

options.text: It depends on the size of the vocabulary

questions.prompt: A toy corpus has an initial base vocabulary of 8 unique characters. If the Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) algorithm performs exactly 5 merge operations, what is the final size of the vocabulary?
Which statement correctly describes how WordPiece chooses the next pair to merge, compared with BPE?

options.text: BPE merges the most frequent pair, while WordPiece merges the pair maximising Frequency(A, B) / (Frequency(A) × Frequency(B))
BPE merges the least frequent pair, while WordPiece merges the most frequent pair
Both merge the pair with the highest raw co-occurrence frequency
WordPiece merges the pair maximising Frequency(A) × Frequency(B) / Frequency(A, B)

questions.sourceAnswerText: BPE merges the most frequent pair, while WordPiece merges the pair maximising Frequency(A, B) / (Frequency(A) × Frequency(B))

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about subword tokenization are true?

options.text: It guarantees that every word in the test set is present in the vocabulary as a single token.
Rare and morphologically complex words are split into meaningful subword units.
It offers a middle ground between word-level and character-level tokenization.
It keeps the vocabulary size bounded while still being able to represent unseen words.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Rare and morphologically complex words are split into meaningful subword units., It offers a middle ground between word-level and character-level tokenization., It keeps the vocabulary size bounded while still being able to represent unseen words.

questions.prompt: Why is Word2Vec training described as self-supervised?

options.text: The training labels are produced by human annotators before training begins.
The corpus itself supplies the labels, since the context of a word acts as its supervision signal.
The model supervises its own learning rate schedule during training.
An external labelled dataset is required to validate every update.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The corpus itself supplies the labels, since the context of a word acts as its supervision signal.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of negative sampling in Word2Vec training?

options.text: To reduce the dimensionality of the learned word vectors
To guarantee that gradient descent converges to a global optimum
To avoid computing the softmax normalisation over the entire vocabulary
To remove stop words from the training corpus

questions.sourceAnswerText: To avoid computing the softmax normalisation over the entire vocabulary

questions.prompt: Which of the following representations handles Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) words best?

options.text: One-hot encoding
Count-based SVD embeddings
CBOW Word2Vec
FastText embeddings

questions.sourceAnswerText: FastText embeddings

weeks.title: Week 5
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: State True or False. Lowering the temperature parameter during decoding flattens the output probability distribution and increases the diversity of the generated text.

options.text: True
False

questions.sourceAnswerText: False

questions.prompt: Given encoder hidden states h1 = [3, 1], h2 = [1, 4], h3 = [2, 2] and decoder hidden state s = [1, 1], compute attention weights using dot product as the scoring function.
What is the primary cause of the vanishing gradient problem in a vanilla RNN?

options.text: Repeated multiplication by the recurrent weight matrix and by activation derivatives smaller than 1 across many timesteps
The absence of any non-linear activation function in the recurrence
The use of a fixed-size input window at every timestep
The inability of the network to process variable-length sequences

questions.sourceAnswerText: Repeated multiplication by the recurrent weight matrix and by activation derivatives smaller than 1 across many timesteps

questions.prompt: Which gate in an LSTM controls how much of the current cell state is exposed as the hidden state at that timestep?

options.text: Forget gate
Input gate
Output gate
Cell candidate gate

questions.sourceAnswerText: Output gate

questions.prompt: Which limitation of the basic encoder-decoder Seq2Seq model does the attention mechanism directly address?

options.text: The encoder cannot process variable-length inputs.
The whole source sequence has to be compressed into a single fixed-length context vector.
The decoder cannot condition on its own previously generated tokens.
The model requires the source and target sequences to be of equal length.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The whole source sequence has to be compressed into a single fixed-length context vector.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a correct statement about the encoder-decoder architecture?

options.text: The encoder emits one output token per timestep during decoding.
The decoder produces a summary representation of the input sequence.
The decoder generates each output conditioned on the encoder representation and on its own previously generated tokens.
The encoder retains only the first token of the input sequence.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The decoder generates each output conditioned on the encoder representation and on its own previously generated tokens.

questions.prompt: Why are RNNs preferred over fixed-window feed-forward neural language models?

options.text: They always have a larger number of parameters.
They can process sequences of arbitrary length and share the same weights across timesteps.
They remove the need for a word embedding layer.
None of the above.

questions.sourceAnswerText: They can process sequences of arbitrary length and share the same weights across timesteps.

questions.prompt:
Which of the following statements about Seq2Seq models are true?
(i) The generation of the target sequence is conditioned on the source sequence.
(ii) In the basic model, the encoder compresses the input into a fixed-size vector representation.
(iii) The input and output sequences must have the same length.

options.text: (i) and (ii)
(ii) only
(iii) only
(i), (ii) and (iii)

questions.sourceAnswerText: (i) and (ii)

weeks.title: Week 6
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: State True or False. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes position by applying a rotation to the query and key vectors rather than by adding a positional vector to the input embedding.

options.text: True
False

questions.sourceAnswerText: True

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true about multi-head attention?

options.text: All heads share a single set of attention weights, which improves interpretability.
Each head uses its own learned projections and can attend to different representation subspaces in parallel.
It reduces the total number of parameters relative to single-head attention of the same width.
The heads are averaged before the softmax is applied.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Each head uses its own learned projections and can attend to different representation subspaces in parallel.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the residual connection in a Transformer block?

options.text: It improves gradient flow during backpropagation and makes deep stacks trainable.
It normalises the input embeddings.
It reduces the computational complexity of attention.
It removes the need for positional information.

questions.sourceAnswerText: It improves gradient flow during backpropagation and makes deep stacks trainable.

questions.prompt: What is the primary reason Transformers use layer normalization instead of batch normalization?

options.text: Layer normalization is always faster to compute than batch normalization.
Batch normalization is not effective for sequence models, where statistics vary with batch composition and sequence length.
Layer normalization by itself prevents overfitting.
Batch normalization is incompatible with positional encodings.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Batch normalization is not effective for sequence models, where statistics vary with batch composition and sequence length.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is NOT true?

options.text: Self-attention allows every token to attend to every other token in the sequence.
Multi-head attention increases the output dimensionality of the Transformer block relative to a single head of the same total width.
Relative positional encoding captures the distance between tokens rather than their absolute positions.
Positional encoding is necessary because self-attention on its own is permutation invariant.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Multi-head attention increases the output dimensionality of the Transformer block relative to a single head of the same total width.

questions.prompt: How does masked self-attention support autoregressive generation?

options.text: By allowing every position to attend to all tokens, including future ones.
By restricting each position to attend only to itself and earlier positions, preventing information leakage from the future.
By discarding positional information within the sequence.
By disabling the attention mechanism during training.

questions.sourceAnswerText: By restricting each position to attend only to itself and earlier positions, preventing information leakage from the future.

questions.prompt: A self-attention layer has input dimension d_model = 1024 and uses 16 heads. What is the dimension of the output of each individual head?
For a Transformer with d_model = 512, compute the sinusoidal positional encoding for position p = 20 at dimensions 4 and 5, using the supplied sinusoidal formulation.

weeks.title: Week 7
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements correctly differentiates the pre-training paradigms of BERT and T5?

options.text: BERT uses masked language modeling with bidirectional attention, whereas T5 utilizes a span corruption objective within an encoder-decoder architecture.
BERT uses next-token prediction, whereas T5 uses next-sentence prediction.
BERT is an encoder-decoder model, whereas T5 is a decoder-only model.
BERT uses span corruption on C4, whereas T5 is trained on BookCorpus using a causal decoder.

questions.sourceAnswerText: BERT uses masked language modeling with bidirectional attention, whereas T5 utilizes a span corruption objective within an encoder-decoder architecture.

questions.prompt: Which attention mechanism and masking scheme are natively employed during the auto-regressive generation phase in a Transformer decoder to prevent attending to future token positions?

options.text: Bidirectional attention with a fully-visible mask
Causal (autoregressive) self-attention with a lower-triangular mask
Prefix-LM mask allowing unrestricted visibility across all generated tokens
Cross-attention with a diagonal identity mask

questions.sourceAnswerText: Causal (autoregressive) self-attention with a lower-triangular mask

questions.prompt: Which of the following pre-training corpora was curated specifically for pre-training the T5 model as a cleaner, highly-filtered alternative to raw web scrapes?

options.text: BookCorpus
Wikipedia-100M
Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (C4)
OpenWebText

questions.sourceAnswerText: Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (C4)

questions.prompt: In the ELMo task-specific combination formula, what is the primary function of the softmax-normalized scalar weights s_j^task?

options.text: They rescale the output embedding dimensionality to match downstream architectures.
They determine the relative task-specific importance and contribution of each internal bi-LSTM layer representation.
They prevent gradient explosion during the character-CNN convolution step.
They linearly combine the forward and backward language model losses during unsupervised pre-training.

questions.sourceAnswerText: They determine the relative task-specific importance and contribution of each internal bi-LSTM layer representation.

questions.prompt: Which model architecture family is natively suited for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as Machine Translation and Abstractive Summarization without requiring structural modifications or prompt-based workarounds?

options.text: Encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa)
Encoder-Decoder models (e.g., BART, T5)
Character-level CNNs with unidirectional LSTMs
Pure classifier heads with static word embeddings

questions.sourceAnswerText: Encoder-Decoder models (e.g., BART, T5)

questions.prompt: What major modifications were introduced in the GPT-2 architecture and training recipe compared to the original GPT-1?

options.text: Relocating layer normalization to the input of each sub-block (pre-LN) and adding a layer norm after the final self-attention block.
Expanding the vocabulary size to ~50,257 and increasing the context window to 1024 tokens.
Scaling residual layer weights at initialization by a factor of 1/√(2N).
All of the above.

questions.sourceAnswerText: All of the above.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements regarding token representations and pre-training objectives are TRUE?

options.text: ELMo employs a character-level CNN at the input layer to handle OOV tokens and capture morphological subword patterns.
BERT generates dynamic, context-dependent token representations using Masked Language Modeling and Next Sentence Prediction.
Standard autoregressive decoder-only models maximize the bidirectional context likelihood ∏t=1T P(wt | w1, ..., wT).
BART incorporates a bidirectional encoder with an autoregressive decoder and trains on noising schemes including token deletion and sentence permutation.

questions.sourceAnswerText: ELMo employs a character-level CNN at the input layer to handle OOV tokens and capture morphological subword patterns., BERT generates dynamic, context-dependent token representations using Masked Language Modeling and Next Sentence Prediction., BART incorporates a bidirectional encoder with an autoregressive decoder and trains on noising schemes including token deletion and sentence permutation.

weeks.title: Week 8
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about instruction tuning of a pretrained language model are true?

options.text: The prompt tokens are masked out of the next-token loss, so only the response tokens are supervised.
It updates the parameters of the base model.
It requires a separately trained reward model.
Training on several different phrasings of the same task improves generalisation to unseen instructions.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The prompt tokens are masked out of the next-token loss, so only the response tokens are supervised., It updates the parameters of the base model., Training on several different phrasings of the same task improves generalisation to unseen instructions.

questions.prompt: In prompt tuning, which parameters are updated during training?

options.text: All the weights of the pretrained model
Only the continuous prompt embeddings prepended to the input, while the model stays frozen
Only the final layer normalisation and the output head
The merge rules of the tokenizer

questions.sourceAnswerText: Only the continuous prompt embeddings prepended to the input, while the model stays frozen

questions.prompt: Which capability does Tree-of-Thought (ToT) prompting add over Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting?

options.text: It fine-tunes the model on reasoning traces before inference.
It maintains several candidate reasoning branches and can backtrack from unpromising ones.
It removes the need for any prompt design.
It guarantees that the final answer is factually correct.

questions.sourceAnswerText: It maintains several candidate reasoning branches and can backtrack from unpromising ones.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT captured by the POSIX metric for prompt sensitivity?

options.text: Diversity in the responses produced under intent-preserving prompt variations
Entropy of the distribution of response frequencies
The wall-clock time taken to generate a response
Variance in the log-likelihood assigned to the same response across prompt variations

questions.sourceAnswerText: The wall-clock time taken to generate a response

questions.prompt: Which conclusion about prompt sensitivity is supported by POSIX measurements across model families?

options.text: Prompt sensitivity decreases monotonically with parameter count.
A larger model within the same family can still be more prompt sensitive than a smaller one.
Prompt sensitivity is zero for any instruction-tuned model.
All models of the same parameter count have identical prompt sensitivity.

questions.sourceAnswerText: A larger model within the same family can still be more prompt sensitive than a smaller one.

questions.prompt: Why is alignment performed on top of instruction tuning rather than stopping at instruction tuning?

options.text: Instruction tuning does not allow the model to follow any instructions at all.
Instruction tuning can still yield fluent, instruction-following responses that humans judge harmful or unacceptable.
Instruction tuning destroys the model's performance on downstream tasks.
Alignment is needed only for models below a few billion parameters.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Instruction tuning can still yield fluent, instruction-following responses that humans judge harmful or unacceptable.

questions.prompt: A reward model r(x, y) is trained on preference triples (x, y_w, y_l), where y_w is preferred and y_l rejected. Using Bradley-Terry, the training objective maximises:

options.text: log σ(r(x, y_l) − r(x, y_w))
log σ(r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l))
the entropy of the policy distribution
the KL divergence between the policy and the reference model

questions.sourceAnswerText: log σ(r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l))

questions.prompt: In RLHF the policy is optimised for reward while a KL penalty against a reference policy is applied. What is the primary purpose of that KL term?

options.text: To make each gradient update cheaper to compute
To keep the optimised policy close to the reference model, so it does not drift into degenerate high-reward behaviour
To increase the entropy of the sampled responses
To remove annotator bias from the preference dataset

questions.sourceAnswerText: To keep the optimised policy close to the reference model, so it does not drift into degenerate high-reward behaviour

questions.prompt: Which statements about REINFORCE-style policy optimisation for language models are true?

options.text: The log-derivative trick yields an unbiased estimator of the policy gradient from sampled responses.
Weighting token-level log-probabilities by an advantage rather than raw return reduces gradient variance.
Importance ratios are clipped when several updates are taken on samples drawn from an older policy.
The reward function must be differentiable with respect to the model parameters.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The log-derivative trick yields an unbiased estimator of the policy gradient from sampled responses., Weighting token-level log-probabilities by an advantage rather than raw return reduces gradient variance., Importance ratios are clipped when several updates are taken on samples drawn from an older policy.

questions.prompt: Let ratio_t = π_new(a_t | s_t) / π_old(a_t | s_t), and ε > 0 be the clipping parameter. When the token-level advantage A_t is negative, the PPO-CLIP objective at step t reduces to maximising:

options.text: min(ratio_t, 1 + ε) A_t
max(ratio_t, 1 − ε) A_t
min(ratio_t, 1 − ε) A_t
max(ratio_t, 1 + ε) A_t

questions.sourceAnswerText: max(ratio_t, 1 − ε) A_t

weeks.title: Week 9
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why a knowledge graph (KG) is a more flexible representation than a traditional relational knowledge base?

options.text: A KG needs no schema at all, whereas a relational knowledge base always does.
A KG stores entities as nodes joined by typed edges, so heterogeneous relations and multi-hop traversal are represented directly.
A KG stores every fact as a hypergraph, which removes all redundancy.
A KG makes textual sources unnecessary because it stores every possible fact.

questions.sourceAnswerText: A KG stores entities as nodes joined by typed edges, so heterogeneous relations and multi-hop traversal are represented directly.

questions.prompt: Entity and relation alignment across knowledge graphs in different languages is a hard problem. Which genuinely contribute to effective alignment?

options.text: Transliteration and cross-lingual string matching over entity labels
Comparing the neighbourhood structure of candidate entities in the two graphs
Requiring every alias of an entity to appear identically in both graphs
Matching relations purely on lexical similarity of their names, ignoring context

questions.sourceAnswerText: Transliteration and cross-lingual string matching over entity labels, Comparing the neighbourhood structure of candidate entities in the two graphs

questions.prompt: Which of the following are learned jointly in an end-to-end differentiable KGQA system, as opposed to a semantic parsing approach?

options.text: A dense representation of the natural language question
Embeddings of the entities and relations in the graph
A hand-specified logical form for each question template
The scoring mechanism that selects which node answers the question

questions.sourceAnswerText: A dense representation of the natural language question, Embeddings of the entities and relations in the graph, The scoring mechanism that selects which node answers the question

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe the local closed-world assumption used when generating negatives for KG training?

options.text: Triples not present in the graph are treated as false during training.
It is strictly correct, because knowledge graphs are complete by construction.
Some sampled negatives are in fact missing true triples, so the training signal carries label noise.
It removes the need for a separate validation split.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Triples not present in the graph are treated as false during training., Some sampled negatives are in fact missing true triples, so the training signal carries label noise.

questions.prompt: A KG completion model uses a softmax over entities to model P(o | s, r). Which statements about replacing the full softmax with a sampled one are correct?

options.text: The exact denominator requires scoring every entity in the graph, which is prohibitively expensive for large KGs.
The true object must be kept in the sampled denominator, otherwise the estimate is biased.
Sampling negatives uniformly tends to produce easy negatives, giving a high-variance training signal.
Sampled softmax removes the need to learn entity embeddings.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The exact denominator requires scoring every entity in the graph, which is prohibitively expensive for large KGs., The true object must be kept in the sampled denominator, otherwise the estimate is biased., Sampling negatives uniformly tends to produce easy negatives, giving a high-variance training signal.

questions.prompt: A model uses hinge loss max{0, m + f(s', r, o') − f(s, r, o)}. A positive triple is (s,r,o), a sampled negative is (s',r,o'), m > 0, and higher f means more plausible. The loss is strictly positive when:

options.text: f(s, r, o) ≥ f(s', r, o') + m
f(s, r, o) < f(s', r, o') + m
f(s', r, o') ≥ f(s, r, o) + m
Only when m = 0

questions.sourceAnswerText: f(s, r, o) < f(s', r, o') + m

questions.prompt: For a single test query, a KG completion model ranks the correct entity 4th out of 100 candidates. What are hits@1, hits@5 and reciprocal rank?
Which statements about filtered evaluation for KG completion are correct?

options.text: Candidate entities forming known true triples in training or validation are removed before the test entity is scored.
It avoids penalising the model for placing a different, genuinely correct answer above the held-out one.
It can only ever lower the reported score compared with the raw setting.
It changes ranking metrics such as MRR and hits@K.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Candidate entities forming known true triples in training or validation are removed before the test entity is scored., It avoids penalising the model for placing a different, genuinely correct answer above the held-out one., It changes ranking metrics such as MRR and hits@K.

questions.prompt: Why can TransE not represent a non-trivial symmetric relation?

options.text: Because the norm of every relation embedding in TransE is constrained to 1.
Because symmetry would require both s + r ≈ o and o + r ≈ s, which forces r ≈ 0 and collapses the relation.
Because the subject and object embeddings would have to be orthogonal.
Because TransE uses complex-valued embeddings that cannot encode symmetry.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Because symmetry would require both s + r ≈ o and o + r ≈ s, which forces r ≈ 0 and collapses the relation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the RotatE scoring function?

options.text: f(s, r, o) = ‖s + r − o‖
f(s, r, o) = ‖s ⊙ r − o‖, where every component of r has modulus 1
f(s, r, o) = sᵀ M_r o, with M_r a full matrix
f(s, r, o) = −⟨s, r, o⟩, the real part of a three-way inner product

questions.sourceAnswerText: f(s, r, o) = ‖s ⊙ r − o‖, where every component of r has modulus 1

weeks.title: Week 10
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: In LoRA, the update to a frozen weight matrix W of shape d × k is ΔW = BA, with B of shape d × r and A of shape r × k. For d = k = 4096 and rank r = 8, how many trainable parameters does this adapter introduce for one matrix?
Where do prefix tuning and adapters inject their task-specific parameters in a Transformer?

options.text: Prefix tuning inserts bottleneck feed-forward modules inside each block, while adapters prepend trainable vectors to the input.
Prefix tuning prepends trainable key and value vectors at every layer, while adapters insert small bottleneck modules inside the blocks.
Both modify only the final output projection, differing in how they initialise it.
Both work purely by altering the attention mask.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Prefix tuning prepends trainable key and value vectors at every layer, while adapters insert small bottleneck modules inside the blocks.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about extensions of LoRA are correct?

options.text: QLoRA trains low-rank adapters on top of a base model quantised to 4 bits.
DyLoRA trains over a range of ranks so that a rank can be selected afterwards without retraining.
AdaLoRA distributes a parameter budget across modules by importance instead of fixing one rank everywhere.
LoRA adapters cannot be folded back into the base weights, so they always add inference latency.

questions.sourceAnswerText: QLoRA trains low-rank adapters on top of a base model quantised to 4 bits., DyLoRA trains over a range of ranks so that a rank can be selected afterwards without retraining., AdaLoRA distributes a parameter budget across modules by importance instead of fixing one rank everywhere.

questions.prompt: Why does unstructured magnitude pruning often fail to deliver a wall-clock speedup even at high sparsity?

options.text: Because it removes entire attention heads and so changes the output dimension.
Because the surviving weights are scattered irregularly, and dense kernels cannot exploit that sparsity without specialised hardware or sparse formats.
Because the pruned model must be retrained from random initialisation.
Because only bias terms are eligible for removal.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Because the surviving weights are scattered irregularly, and dense kernels cannot exploit that sparsity without specialised hardware or sparse formats.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes quantization-aware training (QAT) from post-training quantization (PTQ)?

options.text: QAT simulates quantisation error during training so weights adapt to it, while PTQ quantises an already trained model using a small calibration set.
QAT is applied only to activations and PTQ only to weights.
PTQ requires more compute than QAT because it retrains every layer.
PTQ can only be applied to models below one billion parameters.

questions.sourceAnswerText: QAT simulates quantisation error during training so weights adapt to it, while PTQ quantises an already trained model using a small calibration set.

questions.prompt: In QLoRA, what does double quantization actually quantise a second time?

options.text: The attention weights, taken down to 1 bit in a second pass.
The gradients, before they are accumulated into the optimiser state.
The quantisation constants themselves, that is the per-block scale factors produced by the first quantisation.
Portions of the model that are reverted to FP16 whenever accuracy drops.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The quantisation constants themselves, that is the per-block scale factors produced by the first quantisation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about knowledge distillation for language models are correct?

options.text: Word-level distillation trains the student to match the teacher's output distribution at each token position.
Sequence-level distillation trains the student on sequences generated by the teacher rather than on per-token distributions alone.
The two can be combined so the student learns both local token probabilities and global sequence structure.
Sequence-level distillation requires the teacher to emit a chain-of-thought explanation for every example.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Word-level distillation trains the student to match the teacher's output distribution at each token position., Sequence-level distillation trains the student on sequences generated by the teacher rather than on per-token distributions alone., The two can be combined so the student learns both local token probabilities and global sequence structure.

questions.prompt: In mechanistic interpretability, what is meant by a circuit?

options.text: A pipeline that collects and batches training examples for an autoregressive model
A recurrent module inserted into a Transformer to give it additional memory
A subgraph of the network—particular heads, neurons and connections—hypothesised to implement a specific behaviour
An external tool used to adjust parameters after training has finished

questions.sourceAnswerText: A subgraph of the network—particular heads, neurons and connections—hypothesised to implement a specific behaviour

questions.prompt: In-context copying of the pattern [A][B] … [A] → [B] is attributed to induction heads. Which description matches the mechanism?

options.text: A single head that attends to punctuation to segment the sequence into repeated units
A previous-token head that writes information about the preceding token, composed with a later head that attends to the token following the earlier occurrence of A and copies it
A feed-forward sub-layer that raises the probability of any token seen earlier in the context
A head that masks future positions so repeated tokens cannot be attended to

questions.sourceAnswerText: A previous-token head that writes information about the preceding token, composed with a later head that attends to the token following the earlier occurrence of A and copies it

questions.prompt: In the transformer circuits framing, what do the QK and OV circuits respectively determine for an attention head?

options.text: QK determines where the head attends; OV determines what is read from the attended position and written to the output.
QK determines what is written to the output; OV determines where the head attends.
Both determine how positional information is encoded.
Both are normalisation terms that keep attention scores in a fixed range.

questions.sourceAnswerText: QK determines where the head attends; OV determines what is read from the attended position and written to the output.

weeks.title: Week 11
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly characterise the DistMult model for knowledge graph completion?

options.text: Each relation is parameterised by a full D × D matrix, which lets it capture asymmetric relations.
The relation is represented by a diagonal matrix, so the score is a multiplicative interaction of the entity embeddings.
Because the diagonal form makes the score symmetric in the subject and object, it cannot distinguish a relation from its inverse.
DistMult can only be evaluated on knowledge graphs whose relations are all symmetric.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The relation is represented by a diagonal matrix, so the score is a multiplicative interaction of the entity embeddings., Because the diagonal form makes the score symmetric in the subject and object, it cannot distinguish a relation from its inverse.

questions.prompt: In DistMult, the triple score is the sum over dimensions of the element-wise product of subject, relation and object embeddings. Given s = [1, 2, 0], r = [2, −1, 3], o = [3, 1, 4], what are the scores of (s, r, o) and reversed triple (o, r, s)?

options.text: 4 and 4
4 and −4
4 and 12
6 and 4

questions.sourceAnswerText: 4 and 4

questions.prompt: Which statements about the ComplEx extension of DistMult are true?

options.text: It moves embeddings into the complex domain and takes the complex conjugate of the object embedding in the score.
It replaces multiplicative interaction with element-wise addition of real-valued vectors.
Setting the imaginary part of a relation embedding to zero recovers a symmetric, DistMult-like score.
Every entity embedding must have unit norm for the model to be valid.

questions.sourceAnswerText: It moves embeddings into the complex domain and takes the complex conjugate of the object embedding in the score., Setting the imaginary part of a relation embedding to zero recovers a symmetric, DistMult-like score.

questions.prompt: What is the main modification SimplE makes to DistMult-style models to handle asymmetric relations?

options.text: It replaces entity embeddings with fixed random vectors.
It gives every entity two embeddings, one for its subject role and one for its object role, and learns an embedding for each inverse relation.
It constrains the relation tensor to rank one.
It samples negatives for only half of the training triples.

questions.sourceAnswerText: It gives every entity two embeddings, one for its subject role and one for its object role, and learns an embedding for each inverse relation.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a factorised representation such as DistMult or ComplEx for a large knowledge graph?

options.text: It forces every relation in the graph to be symmetric.
It stores each entity as a one-hot vector, which simplifies nearest-neighbour search.
It collapses the graph into a single scalar summary.
It replaces the full adjacency tensor with low-rank factors, cutting parameters and enabling generalisation to unseen triples.

questions.sourceAnswerText: It replaces the full adjacency tensor with low-rank factors, cutting parameters and enabling generalisation to unseen triples.

questions.prompt: How is a 3D knowledge graph tensor of shape |E| × |R| × |E| commonly reshaped into a matrix factorisation problem?

options.text: The entire tensor is flattened into a 1D array and factorised with SVD.
Each subject-relation pair is collapsed into a single index along one axis, while objects remain along the other axis.
The subject dimension is repeated until it matches the relation dimension.
The relation axis is discarded and the remaining two axes are factorised.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Each subject-relation pair is collapsed into a single index along one axis, while objects remain along the other axis.

questions.prompt: Which property of hierarchical relations motivates specialised embedding geometries rather than standard Euclidean KG embeddings?

options.text: Symmetry: (A, is-a, B) implying (B, is-a, A)
The frequent presence of cycles in a taxonomy
Transitivity: (camel, is-a, mammal) and (mammal, is-a, animal) implying (camel, is-a, animal)
The high dimensionality of the entity embeddings

questions.sourceAnswerText: Transitivity: (camel, is-a, mammal) and (mammal, is-a, animal) implying (camel, is-a, animal)

questions.prompt: Which statements about hyperbolic (Poincaré ball) embeddings for hierarchical data are correct?

options.text: The volume available grows exponentially with radius, matching exponential growth in the number of nodes at each level of a tree.
Distances grow slowly near the centre and increase sharply towards the boundary, so depth in a hierarchy maps naturally onto radius.
Every node must be placed exactly on the boundary of the unit ball.
They give arbitrarily low distortion for any graph, not only tree-like ones.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The volume available grows exponentially with radius, matching exponential growth in the number of nodes at each level of a tree., Distances grow slowly near the centre and increase sharply towards the boundary, so depth in a hierarchy maps naturally onto radius.

questions.prompt: Why can a partial-order approach such as order embeddings suit 'is-a' relations better than a purely distance-based one?

options.text: It encodes the ancestor-descendant relation directly as a coordinate-wise inequality or containment.
It guarantees the full transitive closure of the hierarchy is recovered without any training.
It represents sibling and ancestor pairs as negatively correlated vectors.
It replaces symmetric pairwise distance with an asymmetric notion of ordering, matching the asymmetry of is-a.

questions.sourceAnswerText: It encodes the ancestor-descendant relation directly as a coordinate-wise inequality or containment., It replaces symmetric pairwise distance with an asymmetric notion of ordering, matching the asymmetry of is-a.

questions.prompt: Which limitation of axis-aligned cone embeddings do box embeddings address?

options.text: Cones cannot represent containment at all, whereas boxes can.
A cone has the same measure regardless of how broad or narrow it is, so category size cannot be read off its region, whereas a box has a finite volume.
Cones require all sibling categories to share an apex.
Cones cannot be trained with gradient descent.

questions.sourceAnswerText: A cone has the same measure regardless of how broad or narrow it is, so category size cannot be read off its region, whereas a box has a finite volume.

weeks.title: Week 12
weeks.sourceNote: Questions and answer key extracted from the supplied 2026 LLM Assignment Practice Lab question bank; no course export, account, or submission data is involved.

questions.prompt:
Which statements about bias in large language models are correct?
1. Stereotypical associations can appear in model outputs even when no one involved intended them.
2. Bias enters only during fine-tuning and never from the pretraining corpus.
3. Biased outputs can cause real-world harm by reinforcing discrimination against particular groups.
4. A model scoring highly on standard accuracy benchmarks is necessarily free of bias.

options.text: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
1, 3 and 4

questions.sourceAnswerText: 1 and 3

questions.prompt: In the StereoSet framework, what does a Stereotype Score (SS) of 50 indicate?

options.text: The model refuses half of all prompts that mention a demographic group.
The model chooses stereotypical and anti-stereotypical associations equally often, the ideal value for this metric.
Half of the model's completions are meaningless rather than meaningful.
The model's accuracy on stereotype detection is 50 percent.

questions.sourceAnswerText: The model chooses stereotypical and anti-stereotypical associations equally often, the ideal value for this metric.

questions.prompt: StereoSet reports the idealised CAT score as iCAT = LMS × min(SS, 100 − SS) / 50. For a model with LMS = 80 and SS = 70, what is its iCAT?

Which are recognised sources of bias in large language models?
1. Skewed selection of training data, over-representing some topics or communities.
2. Reliance on older corpora, producing temporal bias against current usage and norms.
3. Over-representation of low-resource languages, producing “linguistic inversion.”
4. Dominance of a few high-resource languages, producing cultural bias in what the model treats as default.

options.text: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4

questions.sourceAnswerText: 1, 2 and 4

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the 'regard' metric?

options.text: A measure of how well a model can explain its own decision process.
The perplexity of a model on demographically sensitive text.
A classifier-assigned label capturing the attitude generated text expresses towards a demographic group.
The proportion of occasions on which a model spontaneously corrects discriminatory language.

questions.sourceAnswerText: A classifier-assigned label capturing the attitude generated text expresses towards a demographic group.

questions.prompt: In bias mitigation with adversarial triggers, what is the aim of prepending a specially chosen token sequence to the prompt?

options.text: To fine-tune model parameters so bias is removed permanently.
To overwrite the model's prior knowledge and effectively reset it.
To exploit the model's existing distribution so biased associations in the continuation are neutralised or reversed.
To randomise token order so the model becomes robust to input perturbation.

questions.sourceAnswerText: To exploit the model's existing distribution so biased associations in the continuation are neutralised or reversed.

questions.prompt: Which steps make up the approach of improving response safety through in-context learning?

options.text: Retrieving safety demonstrations that resemble the incoming user query.
Fine-tuning the model on newly labelled data after each generation.
Including retrieved demonstrations in the prompt as examples that guide the response.
Sampling many responses and returning whichever opinion appears most often.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Retrieving safety demonstrations that resemble the incoming user query., Including retrieved demonstrations in the prompt as examples that guide the response.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the effect of high-resource (HRL) and low-resource languages (LRL) on model training are correct?

options.text: LRLs tend to show higher performance because they are spoken by smaller populations.
HRLs contribute far more training data, so the model can overfit to the cultural perspectives carried in them.
LRLs are under-represented, so the model captures their cultural nuances poorly.
The dominance of HRLs is self-reinforcing, since better performance attracts more data and more investment.

questions.sourceAnswerText: HRLs contribute far more training data, so the model can overfit to the cultural perspectives carried in them., LRLs are under-represented, so the model captures their cultural nuances poorly., The dominance of HRLs is self-reinforcing, since better performance attracts more data and more investment.

questions.prompt: What does counterfactual data augmentation mean as a debiasing technique?

options.text: Generating synthetic examples with a second model and filtering them by a reward score.
Creating additional training examples by swapping demographic terms in existing text, so associations are balanced across groups.
Removing every sentence that mentions a demographic group from the training corpus.
Adding a penalty term to the loss whenever the model generates a demographic term.

questions.sourceAnswerText: Creating additional training examples by swapping demographic terms in existing text, so associations are balanced across groups.

questions.prompt: The idea of a 'Responsible LLM' is presented as addressing which of the following?

options.text: Bias and fairness alone
A set of concerns spanning fairness, explainability, robustness, privacy and security
Only the trade-off between training cost and carbon footprint
The deployment of purely rule-based output filters

questions.sourceAnswerText: A set of concerns spanning fairness, explainability, robustness, privacy and security
